messages.subject: Goodness-of-fit with pcountOpen( ) Dail-Madsen models
parts:
Hello,

I have recently fit a series of candidate pcountOpen( ) Dail-Madsen models and later used AIC-based model selection to choose a model to summarize. After choosing a model, I wanted to evaluate model goodness-of-fit using Nmix.gof.test( ), but I am getting an error as well as several warning messages that suggest parboot( ) simulation issues.

I suspect that the error and warnings stem from the proverbial "N increases with increasing K thanks to unstable NB mixtures" problem, but I would appreciate any additional insight(s).

As one might expect, given >750 sites and 5 primary periods, my set of candidate models take a long time to run, even in parallel on a high-powered computing cluster. It is also important to note that the input dataset involves only 1 secondary period (i.e. based on count data retrieved from a single-visit survey).

The model:
fmList @ fits$fm_gompertz <- pcountOpen(
lambdaformula=~1+log(S)+T+P+T*P+CC+D+LS1+LS2+LS3,
                       gammaformula=~1,
                       omegaformula=~1,
                       pformula=~1+Effort+I(Effort^2),
                       data=umfPCO,
                       mixture="NB",
                       K=200,
                       dynamics="gompertz",
                       method="Nelder-Mead",
                       se=TRUE,
                       immigration=FALSE,
                       control=list(maxit=10000))

Some data/model qualities:
Maximum value of y = 165
Range of predicted p = (0.44, 0.56)
Range of predicted lambda = (3.15, 162.11)

Model estimates:
Abundance (log-scale):
              Estimate     SE      z  P(>|z|)
(Intercept)     7.7791 0.9903   7.86 3.99e-15
log(S)        -8.0038 1.9017  -4.21 2.57e-05
T                -0.4223 0.0363 -11.64 2.70e-31
P                0.0438 0.0400   1.09 2.74e-01
T:P            -0.0456 0.0270  -1.68 9.21e-02
CC             0.4385 0.0387  11.32 1.00e-29
D               -0.0862 0.0399  -2.16 3.06e-02
LS1           -0.0527 0.0358  -1.47 1.42e-01
LS2           -0.1353 0.0341  -3.97 7.25e-05
LS3           -0.0905 0.0324  -2.80 5.17e-03

Growth Rate (log-scale):
 Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)
    -1.94 0.126 -15.3 7.79e-53

Carrying Capacity (log-scale):
 Estimate    SE    z P(>|z|)
      4.2 0.093 45.2       0

Detection (logit-scale):
            Estimate      SE      z  P(>|z|)
(Intercept)  0.24694 0.02784  8.871 7.25e-19
Effort      -0.00244 0.01518 -0.161 8.72e-01
I(Effort^2) -0.02347 0.00717 -3.272 1.07e-03

Dispersion (log-scale):
 Estimate     SE    z  P(>|z|)
    0.744 0.0553 13.5 3.05e-41

AIC: 27913.93
Number of sites: 759
optim convergence code: 0
optim iterations: 138
Bootstrap iterations: 0

Preliminary testing goodness-of-fit:
Nmix.gof.test(fmList @ fits$fm_gompertz, nsim = 3, plot.hist = TRUE, report = NULL, parallel = TRUE, ncores = 3)
Error in environment(form) <- env : attempt to set an attribute on NULL
In addition: There were 50 or more warnings (use warnings() to see the first 50)

warnings()
Warning messages:
1: In rbinom(1, N[i, t - 1], omega[i, t - 1]) : NAs produced
2: In rbinom(1, N[i, t - 1], omega[i, t - 1]) : NAs produced
3: In rbinom(1, N[i, t - 1], omega[i, t - 1]) : NAs produced
...

###

Does anyone have any suggestions on addressing the error and multiple warnings, or should I abandon "NB" mixtures and implement "ZIP" mixtures moving forward? Previous tests suggest that a simulation of estimated Ns with increasing Ks with "NB" mixtures could take weeks to complete, even in parallel on a high-powered computing cluster (i.e. a system that does not allow for weeks of processing). While there are no "0" counts in the input dataset, overdispersion is likely at play (e.g., see above model output).

Based on the {unmarked}, {AICcmodavg}, and {nmixgof} user manuals, as well as Kery (2018) and Knape et al. (2018), it seems that very few operation currently exist to evaluate goodness-of-fit and residuals for pcountOpen( ) Dail-Madsen models.

Thank you for any help in advance.

Best,
Andrew

parts:
Hi Andrew,

Does the log-likelihood stabilize as you increase the value of K? If it
does not, then you should look into an alternative distribution or
modelling approach.

Do you get the same error when you try checking GOF on a simpler model
(null model), using Nmix.gof.test( )? If you do and the issue is
Nmix.gof.test( ), then you can send me the R object of your model
offlist and I can look into it.

Best,

Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Goodness-of-fit with pcountOpen( ) Dail-Madsen models
parts:
Thanks for responding, Marc.

Because of the very long runtimes using "NB" mixtures, I decided to estimate N from multiple null models with increasing K, using "P" mixtures. After increasing K at least 10 times (e.g., every 50-100 units or so, from 175 on up) I would then apply ranef( ) to the model objects and apply bup( ) to their random effects to generate estimates of N for each model. The estimates of N were stable (e.g., numbering ~28,000 in total) across those models involving 10 different increases in K.

I had read on other posts in the group list, that so long as N stabilizes after increasing K several times, then the model results may be considered trustworthy for any one K. Of course, N is not the log-likelihood, but tracking either should be similarly useful; correct? That said, however, perhaps I should not be using "P" mixtures to evaluate this system and assume that "NB" mixtures would behave the same. What do you think?

To answer your other question, I tested whether Nmix.gof.test( ) would work on my null model (i.e. constant dynamics with intercept-only lambda, gamma, omega, and p), but I received the same error message: Error in environment(form) <- env : attempt to set an attribute on NULL, this time without additional warnings. I will send you my model fitList object off list, per your request. Thank you kindly for your time.

Andrew

parts:
Hi Andrew,

Personnally, I would look at the log-likelihood instead of N to check
the effect of varying K. Definitely don't assume that K for Poisson
gives you the same "stability" for NB. For some data sets, I've found
that no viable K value helped to achieve a stability in the log-
likelihood as K increased.

Best,

Marc

parts:
Thanks for clarifying, Marc. I will revisit my model set of "P" mixtures to check their log-likelihoods.
